Where it began

Jacob Bethell was born in Barbados on 23 October 2003, into a family with cricket in its blood: Arthur Bethell, his grandfather, was a first-class cricketer for Barbados. Young Jacob went to Harrison College, and in 2017 he was the best player of the West Indies under-15 tournament.

By then he had won a scholarship to Rugby School, and he moved to the United Kingdom at 12. At Rugby his cricket was in the hands of Mike Powell, once captain of Warwickshire, and in 2021 he made 202 against Marlborough College, a modern record in that annual match.

The player

Warwickshire signed him in 2021, and Ian Bell, who knows a good young batsman when he sees one, spoke of him in glowing terms. He was vice-captain of England at the 2022 Under-19 World Cup, where he made 88 from 42 balls in the quarter-final.

His Test debut came against New Zealand in November 2024, and he made an unbeaten 50 from 37 balls as England won by eight wickets. By October 2026 he had played nine Tests, scoring 579 runs at 34.06 with four fifties and a hundred. That hundred was a big one: 154 at the Sydney Cricket Ground in the last Test of the 2025–26 Ashes.

What made him special

Bethell bats with a freedom that makes the game look a little simpler than it is, and he can score quickly without seeming to hurry. He is a handy bowler too, with eight Test wickets by October 2026 and a best of three for 26.

Early on, the thing to work on was turning more of those promising starts into big scores, which at his age was less a weakness than a list of things to look forward to.

Away from the middle

He already has a remarkable set of firsts. In 2025 he became the youngest man to captain England, leading the T20I side against Ireland. He has made centuries in all three international formats, the youngest player ever to do so, and his first hundred in each kind of senior cricket came in an England shirt.

He plays for Warwickshire and Birmingham Phoenix at home, and for Royal Challengers Bengaluru in the Indian Premier League.

And finally

Most young batsmen make their first first-class hundred on a quiet county afternoon in front of a few hundred people. Jacob Bethell waited for the Sydney Cricket Ground and an Ashes Test. It seems a sensible way to do it, if you can arrange it.
